name: Tallows
description: On the south side of Cape Byron is a long exposed beach called Tallows. A long beach break with loads of space to find a wave to yourself.
access: Beach car park and a few minutes walk.
hazards: Sharks, strong rips and powerful surf.

name: Broken Head
description: A good, occasionally hollow right hand point break that breaks over a sand/rock bottom. Can get insanely good, though it is dependent on sand. Plenty of room to wander up the beach if the point isn't pumping.
access: Park and walk.

name: Kings Beach
description: Kings Beach features a rock bottom covered in sand, and on its day, it can produce fun, playful surf. A decent spring and summer option, it is a rare Sunshine Coast alternative when the winds blow north. Best in small to mid-sized peaky swells.
access: Beach car park

name: Elizabeth Beach
description: Elizabeth Beach faces north and is worth checking in peaky northeast swells or during big stormy, broken up southeast swells. It is fairly inconsistent and requires a big, refracting swell for the surf to turn on.
access: Beach car park

name: Hawks Nest
description: Hawksnest is a popular beach with your typical tourist population. The wave breaks a few hundred yards offshore. There's a reef that sticks up so the wave isn't long before it mushes out into deeper water. One of the best waves on the island when it's breaking.
access: Park in car lot and paddle out to break.

name: Zenith Beach
description: A decent beachbreak that gets good banks at times, Zenith Beach can be quite localized. It’s situated in the Nelson Bay region, just north of Newcastle.
access: Parking lot with trail to beach.

name: Box Beach
description: A reasonably consistent beachbreak, Box Beach also features a left wedge at the northern end of the beach.
access: Drive down Box Beach Road, then walk down the beach access trail.

name: One Mile Beach
description: The sandbars at One Mile don't generally yield a lot of peaky wedges, but can produce fun surf.
access: Beach parking.

name: Stockton Beach
description: One of the longest stretches of uninterrupted beach in the area, Stockton Beach can periodically offer quality peaks depending on the state of the sandbars. In the middle of the beach is the wreckage of a coal ship. A victim of a 1976 cyclone swell, from time to time there can be some good banks either side of the boat, but be prepared to share them with the local sharks. The southern end of Stockton is generally at its best on northeast swells and west to southwest winds.
access: 4WD
hazards: Shallow, rips, sharks, no nearby help.

name: Nobbys Beach
description: With its iconic lighthouse at the harbor entrance, Nobbys Beach is home to a multitude of breaks, including a wedgy left that comes off the breakwall, a sand spit left, a left-hand rock reef, a surging right-hand rock shelf, and finally Nobbys Bank, a sand-dredging left that in the ‘70s honed the legendary tube-riding skills of the likes of Peter McCabe and Roger Clements. Nobbys is semi sheltered in south and southwest winds.
access: Beach car park

name: Bar Beach
description: Depending on the sand build up, Bar Beach can see some good peaks. Expect solid local crowds when it is half decent. A rock reef provides a base for sand build up that can deliver running lefts in a northeast swell and northwest winds. Bar Beach doesn't often hold size as well as nearby Dixon Park, but it can pack some punch.
access: Beach car park

name: Dixon Park
description: One of Newcastle's most well-known beachbreaks, Dixon Park has been known to handle the odd chunky northeast swell. It's one of the more dependable areas for good banks in varying swells.
access: Beach car park

name: Dudley Beach
description: Dudley Beach can be quality beachbreak, but like anywhere, it is dependent on the sandbars. It's best in small to medium-sized swells from the east to northeast. There is also a left rock shelf at the northern end and a hidden right that holds chunky south swells.  Northwest winds are ideal.
access: Car park off Dudley Beach Road

name: Caves Beach
description: Caves Beach features left and right peaks that break over a sandy rock bottom. Caves prefers a south swell as an outside reef between the two beaches blocks northeast swells.
access: Beach car park

name: Catherine Hill Bay
description: Catherine Hill Bay is one of the most consistent beachbreaks south of Newcastle. Due to its halfmoon shape, it is capable of handling swell from both the northeast and southeast. It can handle swells up to 6- 8-foot. It is best with southwest to northwest winds. It is quite a versatile setup, consistent and quite powerful at times for a beachbreak. A bit of a swell magnet, it often has some sort of a sandbar options. The northern end generally has the better banks.
access: Two beach car parks

name: Frazer Park
description: Frazer Park is a fickle beachbreak that generally only handles small to medium sized peaky swells. Anything bigger tends to create too many rips and currents in the tiny bay. It’s generally fairly uncrowded.
access: Beach car park

name: Birdie Beach
description: Birdie Beach can be fun during the summer months as it is protected from north winds. It's a long beach with a wide variety of sandbank setups and gutters. Underpinned by some reef in parts, that can hold some size in the 6ft+ range.
access: car park
hazards: Isolated, powerful surf when the swell is up. Nudists can take you by surprise in summer.

name: Cabbage Tree
description: Cabbage Tree is a north facing reef that's best in northeast and big southeast swells. Featuring both lefts and rights, south to southwest winds are offshore here.
access: Street Parking
hazards: Rocks, rips, locals, sharks, man made obstacles such as the boat ramp (where a nice wave peels on the right swell).

name: Soldiers Beach
description: Soldiers Beach is a beautiful, isolated setup south of Newcastle with a super fun beach-break. The beach is patrolled by lifeguards from September - April.
access: Drive to the car park at Soldiers Point, then walk down to the beach.

name: Pelican Beach
description: Pelican is nice and protected from the prevailing summer northeast winds. It has a rock bottom covered in sand that produces A-frame peaks. A left-hander works off the point in east or northeast swells.
access: Fairly remote beach car park with several long tracks leading to the beach.

name: The Entrance
description: The Entrance is a long, exposed stretch of beach with a variety of scattered peaks. If the sandbars are good, the waves can be quite fun. It can also get quite hollow and heavy in certain conditions.
access: Beach car park

name: Toowoon Bay
description: Toowoon Bay features both left and a right reefbreaks on either side of the bay.
access: Street Parking
hazards: Heavy waves, breaks fast over rocks reef, locals, urchins, strong currents, sharks.

name: Blue Bay
description: Blue Bay is a right-hand reef that has a hollow section and rippable walls. Crowds can be an issue here. For experienced surfers only.
access: Beach car park and short walk
hazards: Heavy waves, breaks fast over rocks reef, locals, urchins, strong currents, sharks.

name: Shelly Beach
description: Shelly Beach offers a left breaking off of a rock shelf and good beachbreaks at the northern end. Surfable in swells from either the northeast or southeast, northwest winds are offshore here. South Shelly also has decent sandbars at times and can hold up in southwest winds.
access: Beach car park

name: Pines
description: Pines is a fun right-hand pointbreak that can offer long walls. On a good day rides can go for 200 to 300 meters. It requires a solid swell to start breaking and is popular with area longboarders.
access: Beach car park

name: Box Head
description: Breaking across a rivermouth-fueled sandbar, the wave at Box Head can go forever if the various sections link up. Extremely dependent on the quality of the sandbar, the break's also very tidal. It really only works on the biggest south swells. Use of a ski or a boat is advised unless you're super fit and can handle long paddles against strong currents.
access: Long paddle or hike. Boat or jet ski is the easier option.
hazards: Boats, skis, sharks, locals, strong current, fatigue.

name: Palm Beach
description: Long, coarse-grained sand beach running around three km (two miles) between a solid rock headland to the south and a remarkable tombola-style headland to the north. This headland, called Barrenjoey, which means “young kangaroo” in the Indigenous Garigal language, is the last piece of the northern Sydney coastal puzzle. Palmy has a variety of wave micro-climates: tucked away in the southern end is “Kiddies” Corner”, an ideal learner’s playground and longboarding haven, while up north under Barrenjoey’s lee is a series of occasional beautiful sandbars, well protected from summer NE seabreezes. In between lies a pile of variable-quality sandbars. Best in an ENE swell and light W-SW winds, but can cope with many conditions.
access: Parking at either end and street parking in between. Easy walks along the beach.

name: Whale Beach
description: The Wedge, at the northern headland and surrounded by Australia's best real estate, is a beautiful, punchy lefthander owned by a crew of very good surfers. There are beachbreaks up and down Whaley, but the Wedge is what you'll be hunting.
access: Beach-front car park. Feed the parking meters too or else you'll get a fat fine. Street parking is free but scarce.
hazards: Strong rips, shallow banks and a tight local crew. Not for the inexperienced when its on. Parking fines.

name: Avalon
description: A classic wave on each headland (North Av on the northern, Little Av on the southern) with plenty of decent beachbreak peaks in between.
access: Beach car park
hazards: Heavy, powerful surf and lots of moving water when the swell is up.

name: Bilgola Beach
description: An absolutely beautiful beach, Bilgola is usually relatively uncrowded—almost like a secret spot in the middle of Sydney's Northern Beaches. The north end is protected from summertime northeast sea breezes. It’s best in smallish, peaky swells. It will start closing out on long period swells.
access: Beach car park

name: Newport
description: One of the most user-friendly reef-sand set ups in Sydney.
access: Beach car park, wheelchair accessible.
hazards: Submerged rocks and reef, strong currents.

name: Bungan
description: It's all about the sand at Bungan. If the sand's good the spot can offer up classic, uncrowded beachbreak peaks. Exposed to both south and northeast swells, the northern end is semi-protected from summer northeast sea breezes.
access: Street parking along the northern headland, steep paved track down to the beach
hazards: Strong sweep and rips when the swell gets overhead.

name: Mona Vale
description: Mona Vale tends to be at its best in summer and autumn. The ideal conditions are east or northeast swells with east to northeast winds.
access: Beach car park, limited street parking. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Warriewood
description: Warriewood can be one of the last places offering rideable surf in howling southerly winds. The setup provides decent though sometimes wonky rights that break close to the cliff base and run up the beach. Although rarely epic, Warriewood can provide a fun, highly surfable option when the majority of the other Northern Beaches are blown out. It can hold solid south swells or small to medium east or even northeast swells and prefers west to south winds.
access: Beach car park and street parking on the cliff above

name: Narrabeen
description: A fine example of a Sydney area classic: the lagoon/estuary opening into a long sand beach. “Northy” is renowned for its long reeling lefts off a sandbar partly constructed by the lagoon’s run-off, but the sand shifts around a lot more than might be guessed, and it’s a spot that rewards long term knowledge and patience. Best in an ENE swell with light W/SW winds, which open up the left’s end section, but can be really good in more south-angled swells too, depending on the state of the sand. Big surf on rare occasions off a bombie reef 400m out to sea. Further down the beach, down toward South Narrabeen, a range of variable-quality sandbars tend to form and dissipate over time.
access: Beach car park.

name: South Narrabeen
description: South Narrabeen is often a straight-hander, but in peaky northeast swells, or even chunky, longer period east to south east swell, it can turn on and produce some super hollow, board-snapping slabs. It's best in west to south-southwest wind.
access: Street parking on small side-streets right on the beach.
hazards: Shallow, jacking peaks can break boards. Powerful rips and moving water on big days.

name: Collaroy
description: Collaroy is a long surf beach that connects to Narrabeen. The southern end is protected from swell and perfect option for a wide range of surfers.
access: Beach car park. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Long Reef
description: The southern side of Long Reef hold numerous options that come to life on south swells. There are multiple outer reef's for advanced surfers as well as a beach break for everyone to enjoy.
access: Beach carpark.

name: Dee Why
description: A dredging right-hand barrel that breaks hard over a shallow rock platform. Dee Why holds a special place in Australian surfing culture. Photography and kneeboard great Peter Crawford made shooting the point his specialty. Also famous for one of Michael Peterson's last surfs. MP saw Simon Anderson on his thruster there in 1981, realized his used-by date had arrived, packed his single fin into his Holden and drove back home to Queensland where he became a recluse.
access: Beach car parks. Wheelchair accessible.
hazards: Crowds, challenging take-off at the point.

name: Curl Curl
description: A 500-yard stretch of beachbreak with an ordinary righthander along the rocks at the southern end. Like Bondi, Curly eats up any south swell, so if it looks flat at Manly (which faces north), drive five-minutes north and you could be surprised by how much swell is around. Hard to get excited about the place - there are far better waves on the northern beaches - but the fact that it's a S swell magnet counts a lot in winter.
access: Beach car park, wheelchair accessible
hazards: Big rips, especially at south end

name: Freshwater
description: A south facing beach that is protected from summer northeast wind, Freshwater Beach is often closed out, but can offer a decent right in the southern corner of the beach, as well as a left that can run back to the rocks. In terms of its relevance to Australian surf history and culture, this is the first place Duke Kahanamoku officially rode the first wave Down Under.
access: Several beach car parks.

name: Winkipop / Fairy Bower
description:
Fairy Bower is one of Sydney’s best, and most famous point breaks. The wave is accessible from Shelly Beach just around the corner, via the car park at the top of the headland. Access is difficult, parking a problem. The reef around the point is strewn with boulders which have an insatiable appetite for foam, fibre-glass and flesh -- not a break for the unwary, even if it looks small from the car park. Breaks very hard and best on two-metre plus NE to ESE swells. On bigger SE to S swells the wave tends to wrap around the point and lose power, spilling wide of the inside section of the reef (called ‘Racecourse’). The outside takeoff pivots around a sucky rock know as surge rock, which has been better known to suck bone dry in big swells and low tides. For experienced surfers only.

Outside and around the corner, is Winkipop, which links through to the Bower on favourable days. A heavy, dredging takeoff and a thick lip provide the cliff top gallery with amusing spectacles of surfers disappearing over the falls, embedded in the lip. A short wave with the rocks very close, one of the hollowest waves on the north side of Sydney. Best in E to SE swells and W to S winds. For experienced surfers only.
access: Long paddle from Shelly Beach, or risk the hop off the rocks. Parking is just on the headland above but be prepared to find parks elsewhere for the lot gets crowded a lot.

name: Bondi Beach
description:
Bondi is the Sydney Eastern Suburbs’ most famous beach. The three-quarter-mile (1km) stretch of southeast-facing sand is very crowded in and out of the water, with people of varying ability on a mix of surf-craft. The northern end is a safe haven for children and beginners; at the southern end, the surf is usually bigger and more suited to advanced surfers.

Thanks to its southern aspect, which exposes it to the majority of swells on this coast, Bondi often struggles to hold good sandbanks. On rare occasions the beach produces good to excellent sand that can handle a solid swell. It comes into its own during the smaller summer months, with a range of banks and warm water making small fun surf for everyone to enjoy. Its exposure often means it'll have waves when the rest of Sydney is flat - and its protection from summer's north-east seabreezes means that while the rest of the city's beaches are being torn to pieces by onshore winds, Bondi is clean and glassy.


LOCAL RESOURCES: Bondi Boardriders | Bondi Surf Bathers Lifesaving Club
access: Beach car park and street parking, both metered and expensive. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Lurline Bay
description: Lurline Bay is a powerful right-hander that breaks over reef. A fickle Eastern Suburbs reef that can hold massive south and southeast swells, it only starts breaking at 6-foot plus and can handle up to 12- to 15-foot on its day. This spot is for experienced surfers only.
access: Boat or jet ski is best, but the paddle from the rocks is doable. Relatively easy rock-off, nightmare getting back in.
hazards: Good luck trying to get back in.

name: Maroubra
description: The 'Bra is a broad, 1000-yard stretch of shifty, urban beachbreak that works best when there's some east in the swell. Some peaks are always better than others, and some areas are closed to surfing in summertime.
access: Beach car parks, street parking. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Malabar
description: Malabar doesn't offer much most days, however, when everywhere else is maxed in the 6- to 8-foot plus range it can be worth checking the left-hander near the cliffs. This reef break is fickle and only works on occasion, but when it does it can provide a rideable alternative on big, windy days.
access: Beach car park

name: Voodoo
description: Voodoo is a complex rock reef platform, sloping rapidly off into deep water and heavily exposed to the south. It draws any swell from this direction, which is Sydney's most common, and when regional beaches are head-high or a bit bigger, Voodoo can be near twice the size and pack a serious, Hawaiian-style punch. The reef is sheltered from the north and thus is happy in any wind from that quarter, including the classic Sydney north-east seabreeze. It's optimum at low to mid tide. The take-off is a gnarly, ledgy bowl and the wave actually grows in size as it heads down the line. A small right bowls off the opposite side of the reef, but vanishes rapidly in larger swells.
access: Sketchy rock-off or paddle through the surf zone via keyhole
hazards: Rocks, reef, urchins, rips, sharks, big powerful waves.

name: Cronulla
description: Cronulla, derived from an Indigenous word — kurranulla, meaning “place of pink seashells” — is located  a half-hour’s drive south of the city. This large sandy southeast-facing bay and dune system stretches for around three miles (4kms) end-to-end, giving surfers quiet waves to suit a range of skill levels. At the south end of the bay you’ll find a variety of point and reef break setups for those looking for a more predictable advanced wave.
access: Beach car park. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Shark Island
description: Shark Island is one of Cronulla's premiere reefs, best in SE swell and a high tide this slab is for the experienced only. It's a heavy shallow reef with a lot of water moving.
access: Street parking followed by difficult rock jump.

name: Stanwell Park
description: Stanwell Park is a shifting beachbreak that generally doesn't handle too much size. It prefers swells from the east or northeast, as well as small, peaky south swells with offshore winds.
access: car park and short walk.

name: Coalcliff
description: Coalcliff is usually a relatively average beachbreak that can be fun and peaky on the right conditions. There's also a fickle left reef bombie at the northern end of the beach that breaks over a shallow rock ledge on longer period southeast to northeast swells. Coalcliff does offer some protection from southerly winds. The south end reef or rock ledge is quite fickle, but will occasionally turn on.
access: Beach car park overlooking the break.
hazards: Deep rocky bay with a reef outcrop that come out of the water on lower tides. Rippy and unpredictable.

name: Austinmer
description: The Austinmer beachbreak is ideal in the 4 to 6-foot range. It is generally best in peaky east to northeast swells, though it can also turn on in small to medium south swells. As a general rule of thumb, look for lefts off the northern end in northeast swells and rights off the southern rock pool/reef in south swells if the sand is good.
access: Beach car park .

name: Sandon Point
description: A perfect right point that barrels and walls and winds down the line and just doesn't stop - Sandon is one of the best righthand points in NSW, a long powerful wave that works well at three-feet, is even better at six-feet, and is superb at 10-feet and more. Sandon looks incredibly inviting from land, and it is, but make sure you don't overstay your welcome, because the power of Sandon is well-known for snapping boards and long hold-downs (even drownings). The wave breaks over a nasty, uneven, weed-covered reef. Another benefit of the wave is that it can handle a southerly wind. When the swell gets some E in it, it will peel all the way through to the beach, jacking, ledging and throwing out as it goes. And all this for a distance of up to 400 meters.
access: car park overlooks the break. Walk down and rock-off.
hazards: Broken boards, dangerously long hold-downs and noodle arms.

name: Bulli
description: An average beachbreak, is best in smaller, peaky swells. Tends to remain relatively uncrowded.
access: Beach car park.
hazards: Beachside cafe can be seen from the surf, so don't paddle out hungry.

name: Woonona
description: Woonona is The Gong's Narrabeen, a real swell magnet that often produces long walling lefts and shorter punchy rights. It prefers east or northeast swells and southwest and north winds. It's a very localized spot with a clear pecking order.
access: Street parking and a beach car park.

name: Bellambi
description: A right-hand reef that's generally soft, Bellambi breaks over a rock bottom. It is best on east to northeast swells. Breaking over a rock bottom, on average it's a mellow, user-friendly wave.
access: Beach car park.

name: Corrimal
description: The Corrimal beachbreaks can be fun in small to medium-size swell. Ideal wind conditions here are west-to-north winds.
access: Beach car park.

name: Fairy Meadow
description: A fun beachbreak that's relatively inconsistent and has problems handling much size, Fairy Meadow is an open, exposed beach that blows out quickly as the wind picks up. Heavily reliant on the quality of sandbars, it's better on smaller, peaky swells and prefers a mid to high tide. It's best in offshore northwest to southwest winds.
access: Beach car park.

name: Windang Island
description: Beginner|Intermediate|Advanced
access: Short walk from a car park.

name: Cowries
description: Cowries is best in east to southeast swells. A challenging, hollow right reef, it breaks over a shallow ledge. It's semi-protected from southerly winds.
access: Sketchy rock jump off, then a short paddle.
hazards: Rocks all over the place and of course they are covered in urchins. Then you have strong currents sweeping you into those rocks. Don't get caught inside.

name: The Farm
description: The Farm is a consistent spot that is south facing and protected from northerly winds. The right-hander breaks over a reef/sand combo and is a mellow wave to ride, making it a user-friendly spot for all kinds of boards.
access: Park up the top and walk down the hill.

name: Redsands
description: Redsands is a hectic, hollow reef break that should only be surfed by experienced surfers. It is a local favorite with an established pecking order that should be respected, it is best in east or east-northeast swells. It's also surfable on massive south swells. Southwest winds are ideal.
access: Rock jump off.
hazards: Rocks, urchins, rips, big waves breaking over shallow rock reef, locals, fishing line and hooks.

name: Mystics
description: Mystics features a series of consistent peaks up and down the beach dictated by the sand flow from the nearby rivermouth. When it’s on it can produce wedgy waves with fast, power pockets and hollow sections. The northern end of the beach has a left-hander that breaks off the rocks.
access: Small dirt car park at end of road, then a walk down a steep track to the beach.
hazards: Very shallow, shifting peaks can slam the unwary. Bit isolated.

name: Jones Beach
description: Jones Beach is best during small to moderate crossed up swells. Very reliant on the quality of the sandbars to produce fun, hollow barrels, at the southern end there can sometimes be a decent right-hander that breaks when there is enough sand built up.
access: Beach car park.

name: Boneyards
description: A sheltered right reef, Boneyards is situated near a headland, which protects it from southerly winds. A deceptive break, it often looks a lot better than it is. Best in east or northeast swells, but also breaks in big southeast or south swells as well.
access: Park on the road above and walk down a grass track to a jump-off point.

name: Werri Beach
description: Immediately north of Gerringong, Werri Beach is blessed with the ability to turn it on in a wide range of conditions. When swells hit from the E, the whole place can light up. As swells shift to the NE or SE, simply shift to the headlands at the northern and southern ends of the beach. Werri Point is found at the southern end, and offers an excellent righthand pointbreak that breaks very close to the rocks and hits you with a big drop before throwing out some hollow barrels. A nice wall offers plenty of room for turns before you set up for the heavy inside section. The beachbreak can also get good depending on the setup of the banks, and can be a great option to avoid the crowds on the point.
access: Street Parking.
hazards: The point can be heavy and hollow on bigger swells.

name: Seven Mile Beach
description: A long stretch of beach, Seven Mile Beach is exposed to most swells and crowds are generally not an issue.
access: Drive along The Lakes Way to scout for waves, then park and walk down to beach once you find a peak that suits you.

name: Penguin Head
description: Penguin Head is a fickle right that really only works during bigger southeast or east swells.
access: Long paddle or jump off the rocks

name: Currarong
description: Currarong has a wide variety of waves to choose from. Protected from south wind, there are reef and beachbreaks all the way to Kinghorn Point. It's best on northeast swells and southwest to southeast winds.
access: A few bush car parks

name: Plantation Point
description: Tucked away inside Jervis Bay, this right-hander only works during the biggest southeast swells. It's a novelty wave when everywhere is out of control.
access: Long paddle from the beach out to the point

name: Black Rock
description: South Coast Pipe, Black Rock, Pipeline, Wreck Bay, Summercloud Bay… whatever you call it, this is one of the best waves on the coast. Black Rock has long held a reputation for providing one of the best lefthand tubes in Australia. There's even a short fun right that breaks until it reaches four-feet. Once you get the wave sussed, it's pretty easy to get slotted - a simple backdoor sets up as easy a tube as you'll find anywhere. It's a short wave, a perfect barrel, and a small takeoff spot.
access: After parking it's a 10 to 15-minute walk. Notorious for car break-ins. Locals keep their car unlocked and leave no valuables, though word is things have changed now and it's relatively safe.
hazards: Heavy wave with a tight pack.

name: Steamers Beach
description: Steamers Beach is a beautiful, secluded spot that can produce fun, wedgy peaks, depending on the condition of the sandbars. It works best in small-scale swells from the south.
access: Isolated beach break that takes a long walk to get to.
hazards: Super isolated, sharky and heavily exposed to south swell.

name: Bendalong Beach
description: A reliable staple for traveling surfers, Bendalong Beach offers an assortment of peaky wedges. This beachbreak is best in small to medium south swells and north to northwest winds. It’s a magnet for south swells.
access: Bush car park
hazards: Swell magnet regularly produces powerful surf, submerged reef at the north end.

name: Green Island
description: Green Island is a classic South Coast setup. Found near the town of Bendalong, the island is located at the mouth of Lake Conjola. You can walk from the beach near the caravan park at Conjola or from Manyana Beach to the north (check it out from Cunjurong Point). Either way, you'll enjoy a picturesque stroll as you watch the waves peel down the side of the island. The walk itself is part of the South Coast experience. It's hard not to unwind as you soak in the quiet country feel of this area.</br></br>One of the best aspects of Green Island is the length of the ride that it offers on a good day. The drop isn't too threatening, but it is quick, and drives into a fast opening section that on the right swell direction can offer some hollow sections. A nice wall provides plenty of room for big turns before the wave moves into deeper water further down the line. There are sometimes hollower waves on offer if you paddle further round the back of the island.
access: A pleasant five to ten minute walk, either from Conjola to the south and Manyana beach to the north

name: Narrawallee
description: Narrawallee enjoys fun, little wedgy peaks. It is divided by a rock outcrop in the middle of the beach and there can be waves on either side. It doesn't handle a lot of swell, but it is reasonably protected from south winds.
access: car park followed by ten minute walk along a track

name: Mollymook Beach
description: Mollymook Beach is a small-wave spot that will start to close out any time it gets over 3-foot. It can have some fun peaks depending on the sandbars, particularly when the swell's east and not pushing too much. It's an ideal spot for beginners and families.
access: Beach car parks and street parking.

name: Golf Course Reef
description: Ulladulla is a mecca for south coast surfers due to the variety of options it provides. One of the best waves can be found by driving through a golf course where you'll find a convenient car park.</br></br>Golf Course Reef is a quality left-hander. Featuring a fast, walling ride that pitches over a sharp ledging reef, it starts getting fun from three feet up, and can hold up to eight feet-plus. Golfies loves a bit of size, and just keeps getting better as the swell increases.</br></br>There are a couple of other options as well, including a right-hand reef just across the bay. This wave will hold sizeable swells and can get almost as good as Golfies. It's a good option to escape the crowd, and sometimes can be good on smaller days with the right swell direction when Golfies isn't working. It can pick up smaller northeast swells and will work on southwest to northwest winds.</br></br>For a hollower option you could try Crystals, but you'll need a reasonable size swell and the skills to match if you want to take it on. This place needs a full-on approach.</br></br>Nearby beachbreaks at Mollymook are a fun option for beginners.
access: Easy access form the car park right on the break
hazards: Locals will want their share when it's on.

name: Ulladulla Bommie
description: The Ulladulla Bommie is a heavy wave with a pitching lip followed by a series of hollow and walling sections that will keep you guessing. This wave breaks on a shallow reef out of deep water and has enough power to slap you down and hold you there.</br></br>Breaking a few hundred meters out in the bay, the Bommie picks up all swell directions and there can be substantial water movement resulting in a shifting peak. It's a relatively simple paddle out through the channel but watch for sneaker sets and a rip that often drags surfers into the impact zone.</br></br>This place likes it big, and it can hold clean swells up to 15 feet. From six feet up, it's unforgiving nature will surprise those who aren't wary as the heavy-water movement and numerous ledges, crevasses, boils and double-ups that make for an unpredictable and challenging wave.
access: Easy walk from the car park
hazards: It's a bombora; you're exposed to the swell's raw power and size.

name: Rennies Beach
description: Rennies has options for everyone. Good in small to medium swells, it can offer consistent rights and lefts. Best in small south swells and north winds.
access: Beach car park

name: Racecourse
description: A quality left that breaks off beyond the rocks of the northern end, Racecourse can get very good but it's fickle. It's best on a mid-range swell.
access: Beach car park

name: Bawley Point
description: Short, powerful wave that has a critical take-off spot very close to sharp, unforgiving, rocks. Experienced surfers only when it's big.
access: Street parking

name: Moruya
description: Several quality waves can be found near the entrance to the Moruya River, a short drive from the beautiful town of Moruya.</br></br>There's a large rock wall at the entrance to the rivermouth and this provides a consistent set up that delivers excellent long rides, mainly lefts, from two to eight foot. At its best, it can break for up to 200 yards, offering up satisfying sand bottom peelers. Another feature is its ability to handle the strong south winds that are common in these parts. The left isn't the only option here either; right-handers can also be had on the other side of the channel.</br></br>On the northern side of the wall you'll find a right-hander that can really turn it on in northeast through to southeast swells and west to southwest winds. This can get as good as the entrance on its day and helps in spreading the weekend crowds. Further up the beach you can take your pick of often-empty beachbreaks.
access: Easy access from car park

name: Congo
description: Congo can be a great beachbreak. The outer reefs tend to help break the swell into peaks before they hit the inside banks. As with any beachbreak, it's all dependent on the ever-shifting sand flow.
access: Limited street and beach parking
hazards: Super shallow banks can slam the inexperienced. Rippy, unpatrolled and sharky

name: Potato Point
description: There are shifting rights and lefts either side of Potato Point. It enjoys wind protection from prevailing north and south winds on either side.
access: Beach car park

name: Narooma
description: The Bar is a consistent right-hander that breaks over the sandbar that's been built up from the break wall.
access: Beach car park

name: Camel Rock
description: If the conditions are right, the long running left of Camel Rock breaks on a relatively consistent sandbar that can be a lot of fun. It runs fast and can get quite hollow given the right combination of swell, wind and tide.
access: Beach parking

name: Merimbula Bar
description: The entrance to Merimbula Lake hosts a perfect lefthand rivermouth sandbar that produces perfect waves on its day, yet can be frustratingly fickle. Merimbula Bar needs a pretty decent-size southerly or SW swell to break, and when it does, if you're lucky enough to be in town, you'll be scoring 200-meter rides with spitting tubes. A fast, sucky, sand-dredging takeoff leads to a series of hollow, wally sections and rippable bowls that will leave you frothing. If the crowd is getting to you, head north over the headland to Short Point to find a beachbreak to yourself, if you're prepared to walk further along the beach towards Tura.
access: Beach car park.

name: Pambula Rivermouth
description: When it's good it's a perfectly hollow, 200-meter, righthand, sand-bottom tuberide. The rivermouth provides the ideal sand setup, all that is required is the perfect swell direction from the NE, preferably the remnants of a tropical cyclone that has slipped down the NSW coast. A tricky recipe in these parts, but when the ingredients come together, you're in for a taste sensation you won't forget quickly.
access: Beach car park

name: Lakes Entrance
description: Lakes Entrance is more of a fishing or tourist town than a great surf stopover. Lots of raw, uncrowded, and often windswept beachbreaks. There is a left reef called Red Bluff well over 100 kms south that can be worth a look, but Ninety Mile Beach, which runs pretty much all the way down to Wilsons Promontory, rarely delivers much in the way of worthwhile beachbreak opportunities.
access: Beach car park

name: Red Bluff
description: A powerful left bowl, Red Bluff breaks over urchin infested reef. Capable of holding 10-foot surf, this is a spot for experience surfers only.
access: Beach car park

name: Gunnamatta
description: Like the beachbreaks of Phillip island, the Mornington Peninsula can get world-class waves, particularly in the summer months when the combination of NE winds and mid-size swells turn it on regularly. From Cape Schank to Portsea, there are over a dozen quality spots offering a variety of beach and reefbreak options. The best and most consistent stretch along this coast is the Gunnamatta area, whilst further west, St. Andrews, Rye and Portsea are all worth checking out - they all work in similar conditions.</br></br>Gunnamatta is a popular spot, and a handful of reefs below the waterline provide stability for the sand and assist the formation of sensational A-frame beachbreaks that can hold up to six-feet. When it gets bigger, and sometimes even on onshore days, Gunnamatta can offer up some fun reforms on the inside. Big rips can tear through the lineup on larger days - these are the days when the lifesavers work overtime and the advanced surfers get some quality waves.
access: Two car parks, easy access.

name: Mornington Peninsula
description: The premier wave on Phillip Island, if you get to surf Express at its best, chances are you'll get one of the barrels of your life. E.P. is a heavy wave. It picks up the full force of any swell marching out of the Southern Ocean and unloads it onto a shallow ledge. Make the drop and prepare to pull in.</br></br>The break is quite exposed, and really only handles a northwest or north wind. Over 6 feet, the drops aren't as hairy and you have more time to set up the bowl section. It's most challenging when you have to take off virtually into the heaving tube section. Make a mistake, and you'll join the long list of surfers with injuries to body, pride, or board.</br></br>The locals have got this place wired, so if you want your wave, show respect and wait your turn, it's worth the wait. Phillip Island has a sharky reputation, and justifiably so, but Express seems to be off the menu, so at least that's one thing you won't have to worry about when surfing here.
access: Walk east a kilometer along the beach from the Smiths Beach Car Park.

name: Point Leo
description: Point Leo is an exposed reef break that has a selection of take-off spots. The wave has changed over time and is suitable for all crafts and ability levels.
access: Adjacent car park, easy access.

name: Cat Bay
description: Cat Bay has two great reef setups. From the parking lot located in the middle of the big, sweeping bay, you can look out over Shelley Beach to the west, Right Point directly in front of you, and Flynns Reef in the distance to the east, with the latter two being the premier options. Cat Bay is worth checking out when large SW swells are able to push around the western tip of Phillip Island. When these swells are accompanied by a wind from the S or SE, Cat Bay comes into its own.</br></br>Shelley Beach is perfect for beginners and longboarders as long, slow swells roll gently into this flat, reef-bottomed left and right peak. Right Point is an excellent lefthand reef, one of the best lefts in Victoria, and is best on an incoming, mid-tide. A nasty, sharp reef means you should choose your exit and entry points carefully. It's a sucky walling takeoff with a couple of rippable sections down the line. When it gets too full, a smaller wave can break closer to shore over the covered reef. Flynns Reef is a fun righthand reef that, like Right Point, is best up to around five-feet and rarely gets much bigger than this. It's an easy paddle-out, and a simple wave to ride, one that provides a short, fun section and a chance to hone your cutbacks.
access: Three car parks, easy access.

name: Woolamai
description: Some of the best beachbreaks in Victoria are found along this golden stretch of beach. From Magiclands at the eastern end along to Anzacs at the west, take your pick from a selection of several A-frame peaks. On a good day, you'll see hollow peaks breaking left and right all the way along this eight-kilometer stretch. The beach continues further west past Ocean Reach and Forrest Caves, and if you're prepared to look around and walk a little, you should be able to avoid the crowd. The handful of reefs below the waterline provide stability for the sand - meaning the chunky southern swells that buffet this coastline don't wash away the banks after every storm. This place picks up a fair bit of swell, and in summer months the standard of surfing is high. Mid-week, in the cooler months, it's still possible to get world-class waves with only a handful of people around.
access: Two car parks, easy access.

name: Kennett River
description: Kennett River is a pretty mellow wave that can be fairly long. Best on lower tides, it also offers some protection from southerlies. It's a good option for surfers of all skill level.
access: Beach car park

name: Wye River
description: There is a small beach at the mouth of the Wye River that can produce some fun beachbreaks at times. There is also a right-hand pointbreak that can get good at times, though it is very fickle and dependent on a solid sand build-up before it begins to line up.
access: Beach car park

name: Cathedral Rock
description: Cathedral Rock is a quality surf spot. It's similar to Winki, but picks up slightly less swell. A lower tide, northwest winds and a solid swell are required for this classic right to switch on.
access: Limited roadside parking.

name: Spout Creek
description: The Spout Creek rivermouth can produce fun left and right peaks depending on the state of the sandbars.
access: Roadside parking

name: Fairhaven
description: Fairhaven can produce fun, shifting left and right peaks that break over shallow sandbars. It's best on small swells with north winds.
access: Easy but limited parking

name: Bells Beach
description: Big, broad, open lineup facing slightly east of south into Bass Strait, but open to the SW, Bells is a short coarse-grained sand beach flanked by old sedimentary rock headlands sloping away to the west and east. There’s several distinct breaks here: Centreside, well up the reef to the west; Rincon or Little Rincon, the tip of the Bells point itself; the Bells Bowl, pretty much the spot’s main break; and Winkipop, Bells’s cousin, just around a short headland to the east. In small swells these spots are all held well apart from each other, but in a big winter-style SW groundswell they feel a lot more connected. Generally best in a SSW swell head-high to triple overhead or bigger, with winds from the NW.
access: Multiple large car parks, easy access on foot. Not wheelchair accessible.
hazards: A large rock known as "The Button" that divides Winkipop and Bells.

name: Jan Juc
description: Jan Juc gets a lot of surf action - mainly due to the fact that it's the closest decent beachbreak in the vicinity of the quality reefs found in the Torquay area. Located in front of the Torquay golf club, Juc can serve up some quality surf when the right conditions come together. Thing is, when the conditions are right here, it's often firing at the nearby reefs. This means a lot of people use it as a backup spot when the swell is getting a touch small or the wind is getting into Bells and Winki. The peaks tend to shift around a bit at Juc, and it can get a touch crowded, but it can still serve up the goods, particularly when the reefs haven't been firing for a while and the locals need to get wet. It's also a useful testing ground for those wanting to practice their air-time in cross-onshore days. When surfing at Juc, keep your eye on Bird Rock, at the western end of the beach - it can provide some short, sucky barrels on mid to high tide. Small takeoff spot.
access: Big car parks, easy access. Wheelchair accessible.

name: 13th Beach
description: Twenty minutes’ drive east of Torquay, this wide-open reef-modified beachbreak zone can be among the highest quality surf in the country on its day. 13th is a go-to for many of the region’s surfers thanks to its swell-magnet status — when Bells is waist-high, here can be twice that. Offshore reefs help fracture approaching swells so they arrive in the surf zone as peaks, rather than just the long walls of Southern Ocean legend. The swells still pack Southern Ocean power, though, and low tide can be a real board-breaker. Best in small to medium SW swells and light to moderate NE-NNW winds. Have a photo for this break? Send it over!
access: Sealed road parallel to beach, several car parking areas, easy access.

name: The Passage
description: Port Fairy can serve up a fun right off the breakwall to the east side of Griffiths Island. It works best in mid to chunky south swells and west winds.
access: Beach car park, street parking

name: Two Mile/Easter Reef
description: Two Mile Bay, also known as Easter Reef, is not for the faint hearted. Just out of Port Campbell harbor you'll find one of Australia's premier big-wave locations. The waves here take a brutal toll on boards, bodies and egos, and you'll need a ton of confidence and ability if you want to match it with the locals when Two Mile does its thing.</br></br>Two Mile starts working when the southwest swells start hitting the 10 feet range, and will break at least twice that size. For ideal conditions, a light northerly will help keep the steep take-offs clean as you sight down the line at one of the biggest walls you're ever likely to see.</br></br>A hard-core crew of locals, regulars from the Surf Coast, and professional surfers in-the-known, keep their eye on the weather maps for the rare days when all the conditions come together for an epic session. If you're not up to it, don't even think about it, just enjoy the show from the cliff.
access: Check your entry and exit points from the cliff top

name: Johanna
description: Johanna is well-known as being a savior for Victorian surfers when the swell starts dropping. It picks up more swell than virtually anywhere else in Victoria. Johanna provides powerful beachbreaks. Around four kilometers of majestic beach is broken up by a combination of nearshore and offshore reefs that provide distinctive sand banks, a must in an area that is buffeted regularly by huge swells. The waves pack a lot of punch, snapping leashes and boards and creating strong rips that make it suitable only for the experienced surfer. This coast usually picks up a few feet more swell than the Bells area, so if Bells is flat, it can still be up to four-feet here.
access: Two car parks, easy access
hazards: Isolated, heavily exposed to large and powerful surf and is unpatrolled year round. Experienced surfers only.

name: Posties
description: Posties is one of the best right-handers in the area. It is best up to about a few feet overhead and can deliver a hollow wave that can challenge even the most experienced surfers.
access: Easy.

name: Waitpinga
description: Head west from Victor Harbor and surf options begin to improve. Just west of Newland Head you'll find two beaches with very similar setups: Waitpinga and Parsons. Both breaks need a reasonable swell to be at their best. In good south or southwest swells you'll find a series of nice peaks along these beaches. Travel any further west and conditions deteriorate as Kangaroo Island blocks any decent swell.</br></br>Good waves can break off the rocky headlands and both ends of the beach, creating long, walling, rippable waves. The beachbreaks can get really good too, providing barrels and fast sections. This is South Australia of course, so you can assume the water is going to be cold all year round. And it means sharks too. Safest bet is avoid dawn and dusk, don't piss in your wetsuit, and don't surf alone.
access: Easy. car park right at the spot and easy access.

name: Middleton
description: On the eastern side of the Fleurieu Peninsula, in the vicinity of Victour Harbour, you'll find several good options for a decent surf. Furthest east is Middleton. The water is rarely clear here, partly due to the proximity of the mouth of the Murray River. Waves here are better suited for beginner surfers, although when the right conditions combine, you can get some quality waves. A series of reefs help break up the beach in one area, and this can provide a more regular peak that can throw out a bit of a lip when it's at its best, and provide fun rides for up to 50 meters. Similar waves can be found at nearby Knights Beach, Day Street and Port Elliot, which can all turn on given the right conditions. Knights in particular can provide fun peaks with the potential for some little barrels.
access: Easy. car park right at the spot and easy access.

name: Pennington Bay
description: Kangaroo Island lies directly south of Adelaide, and as Australia's third largest island, it is responsible for blocking the swell that would otherwise make Adelaide a great surf-city. Being such a big island, and exposed to the full brunt of the Southern Ocean, you just known there's plenty of potential for waves.</br></br>A half-hour flight will get you there, or you can take a ferry across. Either way you'll need a car to discover the secrets of the island. Obviously, the southern coast of the island is the go, with the best spots at Vivonne Bay, Rockies, Hanson Bay and Pennington Bay. On the north coast, when there's a bigger swell, you might luck into some fun waves at Stokes Bay.</br></br>Pennington Bay is a fun beachbreak which can provide A-frame peaks and long, workable walls. It's located nice and close to American River, the major town on Kangaroo Island, and a good place to base yourself for your surf trip. Camping is also highly recommended.</br></br> Kangaroo Island is well known as a great spot for fishing, and for its large seal population. This means the fishing will be good for you too, and hopefully it means the sharks are well fed.
access: 2.5hr Ferry across or 25min flight from Adelaide.

name: Chinamans
description: The decidedly not politically correctly named Chinamans is a powerful wave of consequence with an often vertical take-off. Ledging over a shallow reef, the wave is a thick, hollow left barrel that's not for the faint of heart.
access: Long trek out to end of yorke peninsula.

name: Moana Beach
description: Moana Beach is an average beachbreak that is dependent on the quality of the sandbars. There are also a couple of little reef setups, but they only break during big swells.
access: Easy. car park right at the spot.
hazards: Watching out for beginners and their boards. Sharks. Some rocks.

name: Maslin Beach
description: A series of beachbreaks, as well as several reef options at the end of the beach, Maslin requires a very big outside swell to start working. It was also the first legal nude bathing beach in S.A.
access: Easy. car park right at the spot.
hazards: Watching out for beginners and their boards. Sharks. Some rocks.

name: Grassy Head
description: Grassy Head can deliver a quality right-hander off the point when all of the elements come together. It largely depends on how much sand has built up on the point. And if the right isn't working, the peaky beachbreak wedges further up the beach could be another option.
access: Street Parking

name: Scotts Head
description: A right-hand point break that is highly dependent on the quality and angle of the sand build-up next to the rocks. It’s best on east-northeast swells and south winds. It can be crowded in the holiday season.
access: Beach car park

name: Valla Beach
description: Valla offers a variety of reef and beachbreaks.
access: Beach car park

name: Gallows
description: A powerful left that peaks up on an outer bombie, Gallows has the potential to be a hollow, heavy wave. It can also be very shallow at times. Experienced surfers only.
access: Beach car park

name: Emerald Beach
description: Emerald Beach another of those spots that is largely dependent on the health of the area’s sandbars. It can see some good lefts and does alright even when the north winds start to blow.
access: Beach car park

name: Hat Head
description: Hat Head is a right-hand point break that runs down a rock ledge. Sand can build up along the rock ledge and improve the quality of the waves at times.
access: Beach car park

name: Hungry Head
description: Hungry Head offers assorted beach breaks off the rocks in front of Dalhousie Creek. Scattered peaks up and down the beach can be scouted out if the main break isn't working.
access: Very remote spot

name: Crescent Head
description: Crescent Head is a sand and rock bottomed right hand point break on the NSW mid north coast. It's fun and approachable to all types of surf-craft and ability.
access: Beach car park.

name: Point Plomer
description: Point Plomer, a right-hand pointbreak, relies on quality sandbars for the surf to be any good. If the sand's good, the waves can be quite fun.
access: Beach parking

name: North Shore
description: Another reasonably exposed Sunshine Coast beachbreak, there's a good chance you may be able to score a peak to yourself around North Shore. A bit fickle, the area prefers small, peaky swells with offshore winds.
access: Walk north up the beach from Port Macquarie.

name: Port Macquarie
description: Port Macquarie features a handful of beach breaks/sand bars that are sand dependent and get super fun on their day.
access: Car park. Wheelchair accessible.

name: Flynns Beach
description: Flynns Beach can be fun, but often lacks power.
access: Beach car park

name: Lake Cathie
description: Lake Cathie can produce some decent sandbars. Good waves can be found right along the beach in peaky swells and offshore winds. Check out the group of rocks (Middle Rock) near the southern end that can be surfed on both sides in most swell directions.
access: Beach car park

name: Rainbow Beach
description: Rainbow Beach is an open, exposed beachbreak that has something for all levels. Just keep walking until you find your own peak.
access: Beach parking

name: North Haven
description: The breakwall and rivermouth combination of North Haven often results in a tightly packed series of sandbars that can produce some rippable, powerful peaks. There is often a wedging right that can be found coming off of the breakwall.
access: Beach parking

name: Camden Head
description: A long, relatively isolated stretch of beachbreaks that are suitable for all levels of surfer, the wave quality at Camden Head depends the state of the sandbars. It is exposed to sea breezes and prone to blowing out.
access: Beach parking

name: Kylies Beach
description: A long stretch of beach that can deliver a variety of small peaks suitable for all levels of surfer, Kylies Beach can be fun depending on the state of the sandbars. The area has a lot of exposure to swell and wind.
access: Beach parking

name: Crowdy Head
description: Crowdy Head can produce some fun beachbreak peaks on east or northeast swells, although it is often closed out. This area is sheltered from southerly winds, as well as south swells. This is a good spot for beginners.
access: Beach parking

name: Manning Point
description: The beach at Manning Point picks up any east and southeast swell. It requires small, peaky swells and offshore winds, but due to its exposure, it blows out relatively easily.
access: Beach parking

name: Old Bar
description: Old Bar can get good on its day but is quick to get blown out. It’s a very exposed beach that is highly susceptible to local winds It’s best in small to medium, peaky swells.
access: Beach parking

name: Saltwater Point
description: Saltwater Point is one of the longest rights in the region. It works on most swells above 3-foot. When the swell is from the east to northeast the wave will pack a little more of a punch. Winds from the south to southwest are ideal. Saltwater can be a bit sectiony when the swell is small, but there's usually loads of fun walls to attack, and it can handle a bit of size if it’s clean.
access: Beach car park

name: Diamond Beach
description: A long, exposed stretch of beach that is generally uncrowded, Diamond Beach offers something for everyone from beginners right up to experienced surfers. Wave quality depends on the sandbars. The northern end of Saltwater Point Back Beach can offer some protection from north winds.
access: Beach car park

name: Tuncurry Breakwall
description: When a massive S swell hits the east coast, your options are limited unless you're with a tow team. And that's where the Tuncurry breakwall comes in - 100 yards of classic, hollow beachbreaks on the northern side of the Tuncurry breakwall.
access: Beach car park

name: Boomerang Beach
description: Boomerang is a consistent beachbreak with sandbars at the north and south of the beach. It's punchy and can handle size.
access: Small beach car parks and limited street parking.
hazards: Sharks, submerged rocks at the south end, powerful surf.

name: Sandbar
description: Relatively uncrowded, long stretch of beach suitable for all levels of surfer. Wave quality depends on the sandbars. Quite an exposed stretch coast that is open to all swell.
access: 4WD or long walk from the southern trail

name: Station Creek
description: A rivermouth set-up, Station Creek can offer left and right peaks depending on the state of the sandbars. This spot also enjoys some rare protection from northeast winds.
access: Must drive down long dirt road and cross a few deep creeks to get to the break.
hazards: Look out for debris, like tree limbs, coming out of the creek mouth.

name: Corindi Beach
description: Corindi Beach is a relatively exposed beachbreak that can get good on occasion.
access: Park in neighborhood south of the break and walk north on beach until you find a good break along Corindi.

name: Lennox Head
description: Lennox Head is an east-facing, world class right hand point break. You can admire the wave from above on the large Lennox Point headland before you walk down to the slippery rock off. The 0.8 mile/1.2km long rock bottom point lights up in south-east swells, predominantly occurring during the winter months. It offers surfers quality long green walls with hollow sections depending on the sand formation on the rocky reef. The crowd is heavily geared towards the locals, so if you’re traveling to surf here make sure you mind your manners and bring your friendly face.
access: Two car parks overlooking the break. Unlike most breaks in Australia, you can see Lennox from the main road.
hazards: Heavily crowded on good days. Unavoidable rock off across the slipperiest rocks in the business .

name: Shelly Beach
description: It's quite a hike into this setup, but chances are you will surf it alone. Shelley Beach can deliver a decent left off the northern point and a right off the rocks at the southern end. Tread lightly, be respectful and travel solo or with one friend for company.
access: Beach car park

name: Ballina North Wall
description: On the northern breakwall of the Richmond River in Ballina is a consistent right-hander as well as beachbreaks that stretch 500 yards north. Consistent and punchy.
access: Beach car park.

name: South Wall Ballina
description: A dreamy lefthander that provides, like Tallows in Byron, one of the few options when the wind is from the northeast. When it's on, it's a furious performance wave, especially for goofy-footers like 1999 world champion Mark Occhilupo, who often makes cameos there.
access: A little tougher than the northern headland. You can drive for nearly an hour across the Richmond River and then wind your way back to the headland or take the car ferry from the middle of town.

name: Taronui Bay
description: This is a psycho rock shelf in the Bay of Islands. It breaks both ways and the hardness upon which this wave hits the reef will impress even the hardest of surfers. Drive north to Kerikeri and follow the signs to Taronui Bay, 10 miles north.
access: Secret

name: Mangawhai Heads
description: Located near the rivermouth, Mangawhai Heads can get good peaks depending on the state of the sandbars and what the swell and tide are doing.
access: Easy. Parking available at the beach.

name: Forestry
description: A good option for beginners and intermediate surfers, Forestry is home to a series of beach break peaks and a fun left-hand point break, located south of Te Arai point near Auckland. A beautiful area with fun waves and a relatively uncrowded beach, but still only an hour drive from the city.
access: Drive to the car park, then walk through the forest a minute or two to the beach.
hazards: Sharks, rocks up at the top of the point.

name: Orewa Beach
description: Another beach break within driving distance of Auckland, Orewa Beach is somewhat fickle and relatively soft, but a great wave for beginners, improvers, or anyone looking to do a quick strike from the city. Orewa River Mouth helps spread out the crowd when it gets busy.
access: Do the 30-minute drive from Auckland, park by the Orewa Surf Lifesaving Club, and paddle out.

name: Whangamata
description: Moderate quality beachbreak and better-quality left rivermouth sandbar. Consistent though limited in size.
access: Parking at beach.

name: Mt Maunganui Main Beach
description: Small bay set-up with a range of peaky beachbreaks and a long soft right at the southern end, protected in stormy conditions.
access: Parking at beach.

name: Wainui Beach
description:
Wainui Beach is a quality beach break setup just outside of Gisborne that has been compared to Hossegor and South Straddie, although it can't quite handle the same size as these more famous beach breaks. That being said, it can get quite hollow and produce fun barrels in the chest- to head-high range. Tends to get crowded when its good, especially on weekends. Numerous peaks available, all of which can get good on their day.
 
 
 
 At the northern end is a series of peaks called Whales, the site of a massive sperm whale grave. In 1970, 59 of the mammals beached themselves there.
access: Follow Wainui Road to the beach and walk down from the parking lot.

name: The Island
description: Seven hours out of Auckland is the surf city of Gisborne. There are loads of quality, relatively uncrowded waves around the area. The coast is exposed to an 180 degree swell window, which means options. You'll be able to find The Island by driving to Sponge Bay road out of Gizzy. This is the coast's best wave and features a gnarly left that barrels over shallow reef. Walk out at low tide or paddle out at high.
access: car park. Take Wainui road from Gizzy to Sponge Bay road.

name: Titahi Bay
description: Titahi Bay offers beachbreak peaks that are good for both longboards and shortboards. When it's bigger the north end of the beach can produce some hollow right-handers.
access: Easy, parking available at the beach
hazards: Other surfers, swimmers in the lineup. Rocks at the points on either end of the bay.

name: Lyall Bay - The Corner
description: Lyall Bay is a sheltered cove will work on any south swell. It's a fun spot, but gets super crowded even during small swells.
access: Close parking

name: Mangamanu
description: Many would say this is New Zealand's best right-hand point. If you get it when it's on, you'll find it hard to argue. A perfect, long right point only 15 minutes north of Kaikoura, when its working you'll spot the wave from some distance away. Take your eyes off the lineup for just long enough to swing into the unmarked gravel car park right next to the highway and jump into you wetsuit post haste.</br></br>The wave bends beautifully around a perfectly sculpted sweeping point, reminiscent of Malibu, with an amazing ride to match. At is best, Manga's will serve up rides of well over 200 yards, with quality snap-able walls and several hollow sections thrown in for good measure.</br></br>Even when it's not perfect, Manga's can be plenty of fun, with sometimes up to three different rideable sections to choose from. And if it's not big enough, there are other options in the area, like Meatworks, which can be a pretty classy wave on its day.
access: Easy. Simply park cross the train track and the road, and you're virtually in the lineup.
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Motunau Beach Island
description: Less than an hour's drive north of Christchurch (about 80 km), you'll find the little town of Motunau Beach. You can park in a huge car park near the campground, and a short walk through the trees will reveal a long stretch of beach. Motunau Island, which lies not far offshore, serves to break up the swell just enough to provide some shifting peaks, both lefts and rights. The Motunau rivermouth also helps by providing sediment build up, which can lead to some reasonable sandbars.</br></br>Further along the beach, at the western end, you might be lucky enough to score a left-hand point break, which seems to work best on high tides with a south swell. This stretch picks up a lot of southerly swell due to the aspect of the beach and can handle northerlies pretty well too.
access: Easy walk across the dunes from the car park

name: Taylors Mistake
description: The protected bay of Taylors Mistake produces some fun peaks in smaller swells. It’s well protected from south and north winds.
access: East, parking at the beach.
hazards: Swimmers in the water, especially in the summer.

name: Stoney Beach
description: Similar to its closest neighboring breaks at Raupo Bay (which is just 4 km west from here), and the more popular Hickory Bay (a 13 kilometer drive to the east), Stoney Beach is a beautiful beach backed by a healthy array of stones and rounded rocks. Choosing between the three breaks often comes down to local knowledge of swell and wind.</br></br>Check the swell and wind conditions through your binoculars from the road that follows the crest of the summit of the ancient volcanic rim. It could save you hours of valuable surfing time.</br></br>One of the benefits of Stoney Beach is that it picks up a slightly different swell direction to both Raupo, Hickory and the Christchurch breaks, and as such is often worth checking for a slightly cleaner and/or bigger wave.
access: An easy minute walk.

name: Hickory Bay
description: A session at Hickory encapsulates most of the features that come to mind when thinking of the quintessential south island surf trip: amazing scenery, plenty of driving, the use of binoculars to check the surf from afar, gravel roads, cold water, and a wee tramp through pastures of sheep and their plentiful droppings, and of course, some quality waves.</br></br>Located on the eastern edge of the Banks Peninsula, formed from the twin craters of two ancient volcanoes, the Bay faces southeast and is well protected by high cliffs at both ends end of the beach. From Christchurch it's a good hour's drive by the time you've driven through, up, down and around the Bank's Peninsula. However, it's a popular spot as it often provides waves in conditions that aren't suitable elsewhere.</br></br>You can have a rough guess at the quality of the waves from the sealed road at the top of the ridge. It's worth doing this, as it'll save you the effort of driving the narrow gravel road to the car park at the bottom where you'll need to still to walk a few minutes before you can check the surf. Even then, the waves are over a kilometer away across a farm, a small stream and a driftwood-backed beach.
access: An easy ten-minute walk from the car park across a farm.
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Magnet Bay
description: Magnet Bay will break in most swell sizes, from small to large.  There’s a left-hander that breaks off the point. The best swell direction is from the south. The rips can be annoying when its bigger.
access: Grass parking opposite from a farmhouse. Couple minute walk from there.
hazards: Bouldery bottom can be tough on your feet.

name: Haast Beach
description: The Haast area is situated alongside the Mt. Aspiring National Park, in the heart of the South West New Zealand World Heritage Area. This place is breathtakingly beautiful. Amazing scenery will keep your neck and head turning constantly. Check out the Fox Glacier, go tramping, jet-boating, take a helicopter ride, fish the Haast River, and maybe even have a surf at Haast Beach.</br></br>The beach itself is pristine, as you would expect in a World Heritage Area, and a few near-shore reefs help provide some stability to the sandbanks. Just as well too, since this area picks up an abundance of swell. There are a variety of peaks to choose from…and it'll be a big surprise if you're sharing the spot with anything other than the wildlife that this place is famous for. Enjoy the chilly serenity of a surf in these parts.
access: Easy

name: Blaketown Wedge
description: Check out the southern breakwater built at the mouth of the Grey River and you'll find one of the best setups on the west coast. This place is the real deal, particularly in clean, long period swells and light offshore winds. The Wedge takes its name from the Oceanside suburb of Blaketown, and if you get this place when it's on, you're not likely to forget that fact.  Pulling up at the car park with a brisk offshore and watching the wedge unload with a pristine A-frame, is definitely a sight to behold. From five feet up the wedge can really turn it on. It's predominantly a right, with longer walls and perhaps a slightly rounder tube. The lefts are definitely shorter but can also be punchier and can add some nice variety to your session.
access: Easy

name: Cobden
description: Greymouth is one of the largest settlements on the west coast. It's a town steeped in history, and for those with an interest in the past, it's worth checking out the Maori heritage and the story of the gold rush in the 1860s. Those with a bit more time are sure to appreciate the relaxed vibe that comes from this charming town.</br></br>In terms of waves, just one mile out of Greymouth you'll find Cobden, where you've got two options to choose from, both less than a mile from each other.</br></br>Cobden Beach predominantly dishes up left-handers, while the breakwater just down the road has a tendency to produce rights. Apart from that, the conditions required are quite similar, so check them both out and take your pick. As with most spots on the west coast, you're not likely to have a problem with crowds.
access: Easy
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Nine Mile Beach
description: A long stretch of beachbreaks, with points at the north and south ends.
access: Easy. Parking available at the beach.
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Westport Breakwater
description: Westport is a relaxed town of around 6,000 people, and it's a great base for checking out what the neighboring region has to offer. It has a nice cruisy feel to it, while still providing the comforts you may have been missing if you've been on the spartan west coast for too long.</br></br>The town still operates as a fishing village and functioning seaport, so there's no excuse for not finding a great feed of fish after a fun surf at the Breakwater.</br></br>The waves are located just out of town where the breakwater keeps the entrance to the Buller River in check. Head out past the horse track and follow the road out to the jetty where you can park easily. You can drive onto the beach if you're keen.</br></br>The surf can get great here, left and right peaks that peel and throw-out down the line. There can be a fair bit of water moving around though, due to it being a river mouth and the fact that it also gets quite a big tidal range happening. It's definitely a spot worth checking out on any west coast tour.
access: Easy access, jump off the rocks to avoid a paddle out.

name: Little Wanganui
description: If you're heading north from Westport, it's close to 70 miles before you'll get to enjoy your first glimpse of Little Wanganui as the highway swings sharply towards the coast as you cross the Little Wanganui River. The river's got some great trout fishing, and you'll find plenty of whitebait in this, and all of the rivers of the Karamea region.</br></br>The rivermouth is a good place to start looking for a peak. It can get some good sandbars forming from the sediment build up. The beach stretches off to the north for quite some distance, with the road running parallel alongside it, meaning you can cruise slowly and spot the best peaks without too much difficulty. The town of Karamea is located at the northern end of this stretch of beach.
access: Very easy
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Stent Road
description: This is the best wave on the Taranaki Coast - a top-shelf righthand pointbreak about six hours south of Auckland and four north of Wellington. Paddle out and you'll be fronted with an intense takeoff followed by a fast wall. Barrels and big, heavy waves are the norm here.
access: Easy.

name: Raglan
description: Raglan has three separate points - Indicators, Whale and Manu - plus a series of beachies. The waves are world-class and consistent.
access: Beach car parks, street parking
hazards: Entry and exit in big surf

name: Raglan Manu Bay
description: Manu Bay is the inside surf zone at Raglan. It's the easiest to access and the most approachable wave, so tends to draw a wide range of surfers. A ledgey, sometimes hollow takeoff zone quickly devolves into a longish rolling left with plenty of room for turns.
access: Beach carpark
hazards: Entry and exit during bigger swells

name: Whangapoua Bay
description: No trip to the Antipodes is complete without a week or a month or a year wallowing in the splendor of Great Barrier Island. Dial up Google Earth, punch in the coordinates for Whangapoua, look at the set-up (long sandbar right) and tell us you don't want to jump on a flight tonight.
access: Fly in via light plane. Land at Okiwi airstrip.
hazards: Wearing out your arms after a long right.

name: Muriwai Beach
description: A popular beach break with an adjacent left-hand point, Muriwai is located on the west coast of the North Island, a short drive from Auckland. Tends to get crowded, but the beach is long enough that you can often find your own peak. Mind the rips, as they can be pretty strong.
access: Park near the golf course and walk down to the beach.
hazards: Sharks, rips, backwash at the point.

name: Piha
description: Two black-sand beaches separated by a giant hunk of earth called Lion Rock, there's a good left at the south end, lefts and righthand double-ups off Lion Rock, and peaks to the north.
access: Easy.
hazards: Turning your back on the ocean.

name: Shipwreck Bay
description: This is the best break in the Ahipara area - a long lefthander breaking over sand and rock. Stay a few days and you are almost guaranteed waves. Get the place going off, and you could be in for three-minute rides. The wave has sections for all types of surfers.
access: Four-wheel-drive or a long walk.

name: St. Vincent Pass
description: One of New Caledonia's longer waves, but less consistent and a bit out of the way. Still, this is one perfect wave, and if you catch it good, chances are you'll claim it to be New Caledonia's best spot. It's more of a performance wave, with ample opportunity for any maneuver you fancy, but there are a few barrels here and there. Lips aren't too thick and waves don't break too hard, so St. Vincent is more user-friendly than many New Caledonian passes.
access: Boat trip.

name: False Pass
description: It's called "False Pass" because it really does look like a pass, but it really isn't. It's actually an indentation along the barrier reef that, from sea, looks like it would allow entry into the lagoon. It doesn't, but it can create a barreling left, always catching more swell than anywhere else. It's worth a check on small, windless days. It's not a very long wave, but barrels are the go here. The reef is shallow and sharp, so surf with caution. A consistent, fun, reliable spot that's never totally flat, but it can't hold a lot of swell either.
access: Boat trip.

name: Dumbea Right
description: Shallow and short, but perfect and hollow, the Dumbea Right is a fun and consistent setup. If Dumbea Left is crowded, most likely the right will be either vacant or lightly surfed. Takeoffs are generally steep and deep, blasting into a nice wall/shoulder, ending in the shallow channel. It's not too powerful, but the reef is quite sharp and it's right there underneath you. It's also one of New Caledonia's few right-handers.
access: Boat trip

name: Dumbea Left
description: One of New Caledonia's most classic waves, a long, refined left-hand reef pass with several different sections, from barrels, to air sections, to fat shoulders, to pedal-to-the-medal walls, Dumbea Left has it all. It also has a bit of a crowd problem, but since the lineup is so large and there is more than one take-off zone, there's generally room for everybody. It's not really a dangerous wave as the reef is fairly deep and manageable, but there is always the chance of hitting coral if you get pitched or surf too far inside. Basically, Dumbea Left is a smaller, mellower version of Fiji's Cloudbreak.
access: Boat trip.
hazards: Turning your back to the ocean.

name: Skate Park/Boulari Pass
description: A shallow left-hand reef in the middle of a wide pass, inside the lagoon, producing thick and hollow waves surrounded by nothing but water. Swells roll through the pass and bend around this reef, facing into the trade wind, so it's usually offshore and a bit smaller than other nearby reef passes. But this is a very heavy wave that never closes out and is quite treacherous when it is small due to the reef hazards. On medium-sized days it is more of a hot-dog wave with lots of barrels thrown in for good measure. One of New Caledonia's most consistent waves, and within decent proximity to Noumea.
access: Boat trip

name: Frigate Pass
description: One of Fiji's most famous waves, and also one of the gnarliest, this is the sort of reef pass that if you showed up on the wrong day, you would question its designation as an actual surf spot.
